Thanks for your comments on our explanation. I think we broadly agree on many of the points you raised. You are correct in both cases: our B-matrix does miss the $\epsilon^{-1}$ on all elements except $W_K$; and our C-matrix is missing identities above the upper diagonal. In fact, the $W_{1}$ block should actually be in the lowest left block as well. Thanks for spotting this, the correct $(A, B, C)$ are re-stated below:

$A = {\rm blockdiag}(0,-\epsilon^{-1} I,\ldots, -\epsilon^{-1} I)$

$B = {\rm blockdiag} (W_K, \epsilon^{-1} W_{K-1}, \ldots, \epsilon^{-1} W_2)$

 $C = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & I & 0 & \dots & 0 \\\ 0 & 0 & I & \dots & 0 \\\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & I \\\ W_{1} & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
 
The remaining questions were:
 
**By substituting the above $(A,B,C)$ into the current condition $\mu((A+BJ_{\Phi}C)^{[k]})\leq -\eta$, the problem of learning MLP for $f$ is solved?** 

The answer to this is "approximately" since the above (A,B,C) only approximates an MLP for non-zero $\epsilon$. However, we would say that this analysis highlights our model is more general than an MLP since approximating an MLP is only a special case of the Lurie network.
 
**Can we encode some sparsity $(A,B,C)$ into the parametrisation?** 

This is a good point and the answer is "probably" but it needs some more thought. The main appeal of the parametrisation we have proposed in Theorem 6 is that it removes constraints, whereas encoding sparsity would introduce constraints. However, with appropriate partitioning it would probably be possible to include sparsity and get the best of both worlds.
 
**...it might be an ill-conditioned problem to learn the above $(A,B,C)$ due to $\epsilon^{-1}$.**

 We would emphasize that we are not necessarily proposing the $\epsilon$-parametrised realisation (A,B,C) as a structure to be optimised. Rather, we used this parametrisation to (hopefully) convince you that it is possible to capture an MLP-type structure using the Lurie network i.e. if the training "decided" that this structure was optimal, then it is free to choose it. However, in general the training would probably not settle on the restricted structure of the $\epsilon$-parametrised (A,B,C) matrices, but would choose something more general.  
 
We have a question for you: would you like to see some discussion of the above in the revised paper?

**The notation 1e−5 is not a scientific notation (although it's used a lot in code), instead please use 1x10-5.**

Thank you for pointing this out, we have corrected this in the manuscript. 

**How was the roll-out during the training done? I'm assuming it's using some ODE solver, but the details of ODE solver used is not present in the paper.**

We used Euler integration as is done in Refs. 2,3. Of course, other integration schemes could be used. We have also added some details about this to Section 5.

**The values in Table 1 is unclear. In each cell, there are 2 rows. I assume the first row represents the mean and std of the MSE loss on test set, but the values on the 2nd row of each cell has unclear meaning. What are those?**

These were the best MSE losses on the test set across the N runs. We tried to indicate this in the column title, but we have now added a sentence to the Table 1 caption to make this clearer.

**Related to weakness #3 above, is there a way for Lurie networks to remove the need for prior knowledge of the values of k?**

Please refer to the earlier response to weakness #3.
Thank you for your reply. I will increase my score to 5. I am happy to increase my score to 6 if the authors can provide further convincing results on large-scale experiments.

summary.value: This paper proposes a new architecture for modeling dynamical systems and continuous-time recurrent neural networks. The architecture is theoretically proven to be stable using the k-contraction theoretical framework. The architecture is applied to toy ODEs and compared to other Neural ODE and continuous time architectures.

strengths.value:
Constructing networks to be stable from the ground-up and theoretically proven to be stable is always welcome.

The methodology for carefully constructing test trajectories is sound; this is a detail that is often overlooked.

weaknesses.value:
The paper is impacted by presenting only very simple example problems. The experiments are applied to 3 degree of freedom first order ODEs that are arbitrary and not very commonly studied. The models only have 87 parameters. Trivial problems are good if the main contribution of the paper is a key insight about ML. However, the paper purports itself to demonstrate a new architecture that is proven to be superior with empirical demonstration of superior performance. For that type of claim, “serious” benchmarks for systems that are difficult to learn, due to stiffness or complexity, are required. E.g., Lipschitz RNN did sequential MNIST, audio prediction, and adversarial robustness.

Further, the problems are so small and simple that the proofs do not seem relevant. None of the problems demonstrate the necessity or improvement of the architecture. Would a naive model not be able to learn those systems? How are graph neural networks relevant to problems with only 3 dimensions? Connectivity in that case is trivial.

A minor flaw that could be fixed easily: The datasets are designed by integrating the Euler method. The accuracy of the training data construction was not discussed, nor time step size. This probably indicates that the ground truth solutions used as training data are actually quite inaccurate, and the model is not learning the actual dynamical, i.e. they are just overfitting to very simple algebraic recurrences. A much more accurate integrator would have to be used to generate the data (standard is Dormand-Prince, ode45, with a very small tolerance), or, alternatively, problems with analytical solutions, such as the nonlinear pendulum. The nonlinear pendulum in xy coordinates is a good tough benchmark problem because it is very stiff, has an embedded constraint, has different cycles of attraction, is energy conserving, and has 4 dimensions, and has an analytical solution.

questions.value:
- Significant details on how the model is trained are missing. What are the hyperparameters of the architecture? What is the loss function? What are the labels that are used? Is the label dx/dt, or is the loss function on next timestep prediction? Which ML libraries are used? What is the HPC system that was used? CPUs/GPUs/TPUs?
- Page 3: What is y?
- What is \Phi? and \phi? Its definition seems to change.

comment.value:
**The experiments in this work use very tiny networks. The largest one only has 983 parameters.**

Before the end of the discussion period, we hope to add a larger graph coupled Hopfield Network as an example which will require larger models and hopefully alleviate some of the concerns regarding scalability. This example is motivated by the interaction between different brain areas as highlighted in Ref. 2.

**How are graph neural networks relevant to problems with only 3 dimensions? Connectivity in that case is trivial.**

This is true and is the reason the Graph Lurie Network is not deployed on those examples. We plan to add a larger graph coupled Hopfield Network as an example which we hope will alleviate some of the concerns regarding scalability and will also demonstrate the utility of the Graph Lurie Network. This example is motivated by the interaction between different brain areas as highlighted in Ref. 2.

**A minor flaw that could be fixed easily: The datasets are designed by integrating the Euler method. The accuracy of the training data construction was not discussed, nor time step size. This probably indicates that the ground truth solutions used as training data are actually quite inaccurate, and the model is not learning the actual dynamical, i.e. they are just overfitting to very simple algebraic recurrences. A much more accurate integrator would have to be used to generate the data (standard is Dormand-Prince, ode45, with a very small tolerance), or, alternatively, problems with analytical solutions, such as the nonlinear pendulum. The nonlinear pendulum in xy coordinates is a good tough benchmark problem because it is very stiff, has an embedded constraint, has different cycles of attraction, is energy conserving, and has 4 dimensions, and has an analytical solution.**

With respect, we did not quite understand this comment. It is of course true that the Dormand-Prince ODE solver is more accurate and versatile than the Euler approach, but the latter seemed sufficient for our needs here – as indicated by the experimental results where our model was able to predict precisely the equilibria expected.

**It seems like prior knowledge of the dynamics of the modelled system needs to be known (i.e., whether it's k=1-contracting, k=2, or k=3). This makes it hardly applicable as we would not know the dynamics of most systems of interest.**

Nothing is assumed about the specific dynamics of the system, except a notion of whether it is expected to be 1, 2 or 3-contracting. We would argue that less general assumptions have been made in existing work -see references in general response, where 1-contraction was tacitly assumed. 

Furthermore, if the value of k was unknown, then the values of interest are k=1,2,3, so it is a relatively small space to perform a hyperparameter sweep over. We would also like to re-emphasise the robustness and generalisation benefits of our approach; these are gained through this trade-off. For example, Figs. 7, 8, 9 highlight this, as even the Neural ODE doesn’t learn the correct long-term behaviour, particularly when the initial condition is subject to noise and/or outside the training data.

We thank the reviewer for their insight and thought provoking review.

**Most applications of neural ODE in deep learning do not care the properties of converging to a single or a few equilibrium points. Even for those stable LSSM, the Hippo matrix construction ensures that the model converges very slow in order to achieve long-range memory. From my understanding, the model in this work may have fast converging behaviors, and thus it could suffer from the vanishing gradient issue.**

We are purposefully limiting the domain of application to time-invariant dynamical systems as, to the best of our knowledge, many of the recurrent architectures are not well designed for this setting (see general response and Section 6, paragraph 1). In this application domain, properties of convergence are important, as motivated by the whole field of Control Theory as well as other examples such as those used in Section 5.

The fact several of the sequential processing models (e.g. Refs. 3,4) were designed to address the vanishing/exploding gradient problem is what limits the expressivity of these models for this application. Solutions to this problem typically involve trying to keep the real component of the Jacobian’s eigenvalues close to zero so the gradients grow/decay slowly over long time sequences (for more details on this, see https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.5063); however, this is prohibitive if the system one is trying to model decays/grows quickly. 
 
 As we essentially ignored the vanishing/exploding gradient problem, we were also concerned this might be an issue. However, since we are assuming convergence and encoding it into our model, we were able to train on shorter sequences which we believe is why no issues related to this problem when encountered during training of the model.

- Please see the general response above regarding the addition of the larger problems.

- Re training loss: labels are the sampled sequence $\{x_{1}, x_{2}, ..., x_{T}\}$ and the input is $x_{0}$. This is different to next step prediction. We have tried to make this clearer within the paper as well.

The main issues here are (i) that the reviewer is unconvinced by our previous response where we tried to show how networks could be cascaded to provide a deeper network; and (ii) the lack of a $D$ matrix in our system representation. We try to address both of these points below.

i. In the reviewer's notation we have $\dot{x} = Ax + B \Phi(Cx) =: f(x)$ as a special case of the Lurie network (excluding biases). Take a specific instance of this

$\dot{x}_1 = A_1x_1 + B_1 \Phi(u_1) = f_1(x)$

Let us suppose this is a shallow network. Then if we consider another shallow network

 $\dot{x}_2 = A_2x_2 + B_2 \Phi(u_2) = f_2(x)$

we can connect these two networks with $u_1=C_1 x_2$ and $u_2 = C_2 x_1$ to obtain a deeper network which is precisely of the form $\dot{x}=f(x)$ above. We can continue this cascade via

 $\dot{x}_K = A_K x_K + B_K \Phi(u_K)$ 

with $u_K=C_K x_{K-1}$, $u_1 =C_1 x_K$ to obtain an arbitrarily layered network of the form $\dot{x}=f(x)$.

ii. The reviewer doubts the expressivity of the network since 
$\hat{f}(x) := W_K \Phi (W_{K-1}\Phi(\cdots \Phi(W_1 x)))$ 
cannot be written as  $f(x) = Ax + B \Phi (Cx)$. However, note that $\dot{x}=\hat{f}(x)$ can be written as Equation 1:

$\dot{x} = 0 x + W_{K} \Phi(u_{K-1})$

$u_{K-1} = 0 x  + W_{K-1} \Phi (u_{K-2})$

 ;;;

$u_{2} = 0 x  + W_{2} \Phi (u_{1})$

$u_1 = W_1 x$

Defining $u = [u_{K-1} \dots u_{1}]'$ and the matrices $A,B,C,D$ as

 $A = 0$, $B= [W_K, 0, ..., 0]$, $C = [0, ..., 0, W_1]'$ and D is a block matrix with $W_{K-1}, \dots, W_{2}$ above the main diagonal.
 
The system can be represented as the Lurie system (which the reviewer also equivalently refers to as a neural ODE)

$\dot{x} = Ax + B \Phi(u), \quad u = Cx + D \Phi(u)$

As the reviewer correctly points out the assumption in our work is that $D=0$. However note that a very similar way of writing $\dot{x}=\hat{f}(x)$ is Equation 2:

$\dot{x} = 0 x + W_{K} \Phi(u_{K-1})$

$\epsilon \dot{u}_{K-1} = -u_{K-1} + W_{K-1}\Phi (u_{K-2})$
 
;;;

$epsilon \dot{u}_{2} = -u_{2} + W_{2}\Phi (u_{1})$

$u_1 = W_1 x $

Note as $\epsilon \rightarrow 0$, the representation (Eq. 2) approaches that of (Eq. 1) with $D \neq 0$. Adding the `memory' $\epsilon$ is of course a typical way to ``break'' the algebraic loop present in implicit state-space systems. Representation (Eq. 2) has the equivalent state-space matrices of

$A = {\rm blockdiag}(0,-\epsilon^{-1} I,\ldots, -\epsilon^{-1} I)$

$B = {\rm blockdiag} (W_K,W_{K-1},\ldots,W_2)$

 $C = {\rm blockdiag} (W_1,0,\ldots,0)$

 $D = 0$

which of course has the form $\dot{x}=f(x)$. The nice thing about this form of Lurie system is, under the assumption that $\Phi(\cdot)$ is Lipschitz, that solutions are guaranteed to exist. For a non-zero $D$ term, solutions to $\dot{x} =\hat{f}(x)$ may not exist, so some care has to be taken when using such a model. Some disussion of this may be found in [1].

[1] https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/10155284

We could add a brief summary of the points above to the paper if the reviewer thinks it would be useful?

> We agree, the Lurie Network does not allow external inputs. However, by imposing further structure on the model parameters, in a similar manner to the Graph Lurie Network, one could construct a Lurie Network where the output of one layer influences another. Consider a cascade connection of two Lurie Networks defined by:
A = blockdiag(A1, A2), B = blockdiag(B1, B2), C = [0, C2; C1, 0]
In the above, the matrices (A1,B1,C1) represent the dynamics of the first layer and (A2,B2,C2) the dynamics of layer 2. With this structure, the output from layer 1 is influencing layer 2 as the input to the nonlinearity. The output of layer 2 is also influencing layer 1 through the same mechanism. Additional layers can be cascaded in a similar fashion.

The cascade connection just represents a bigger system, but it is still a closed system where it does not take external inputs. For example, how does one would use Lurie network to represent a pendulum with time-varying external torque $u(t)$?

> the Lurie Network is a generalisation of these models specifically when modelling time-invariant dynamical systems (which implies the external input u(t) is replaced by a bias term)

The other models (that takes external inputs $u(t)$) can also be seen as time-invariant if we include the external inputs $u(t)$ in the shift.

My concern with it not being able to handle external inputs is that its applicability becomes severely limited. For example, it can't be applied to robotics applications as it would need to incorporate external force/torque from motors. Also, unlike LSSM, it can't be applied to non-physics systems, for example just to perform sequence classifications or sequence-to-sequence mapping.

> We hope to add a higher dimensional example of a graph-coupled Hopfield Network before the end of the discussion period, which will hopefully address some of the scalability concerns.

I'm waiting for that :)

1. In comparison to the MLP in your example, the Neural ODE still needs to perform the time domain integration for each batch. This will require significantly more compute compared to updating an MLP trained on MNIST. How many parameters would you have liked to see us use for the Neural ODE?
2. As you have pointed out before, since our models are single layer the number of parameters are all dependent on the dimension of the state. How would you propose we handle this?
3. Did you have a dataset in mind?

I have read the response of the authors and other discussions, and the revisions. The revisions have clarified some minor points, but have not addressed the most significant limitations of the current draft. As such, I choose to keep my score. Detailed response below:

- Larger problems are required. The empirical problems are not bad in of themselves, but as only the bare minimum toy problems. There is still no empirical result that depends on the discussion about graph neural networks. This is an interesting direction, but this submission is incomplete as of this point.
- Re. forward euler: The forward euler integration of ODE problems means that the training datasets are not an accurate depiction of the actual systems. A low accuracy integrator may produce trajectories that look okay visually and have the same stationary points, but, for use as a training target, the low accuracy “leaks” into the model. As a discretized system, the forward euler equation creates a much simpler algebraic recurrence than the actual ODE trajectory. The discrete problems being learned may thus have slightly different properties, such as being much easier to learn or having different stiffness properties. It is important to take a lot more care and consideration into constructing your training data. It is necessary to carefully use high order integrators to “overkill” the accuracy for synthesizing ML datasets, or to consider problems with analytical solutions. Of course, this is not an issue when using actual real-world datasets, though measurement noise becomes a factor then. 
- Re. training loss: MSE with which label? f(x) = x(t+Dt), or f(x) = dx/dt(t)?

We agree that accounting for feedforward neural networks would be a further enhancement, but we still believe the model we have proposed represent such functions, as argued in our previous response. 

We would also agree that the SDP formulation, as in Theorem 3, follows simply from the fundamental result of Wu et al; however, due to the compound matrix operator, this required the simplification C = B^{-1}, rendering the result impractical. This same difficulty would be present in $\mu( (A+W_{K} J_{K} W_{K−1} \dots J_{1} W_{1})^{[k]}) \leq -\eta$ which we believe to be an advantage of our representation. We would like to add that Theorem 2 on the other hand, is not such a simple extension of this result and this is the Theorem which was used in practice.
Thank you for this helpful discussion. We are in the process of adding the new experimental results to the paper.

I am not convinced by the new experimental results. Now I am quite skeptical about the scalability of the Lurie Net. I will keep my score to 5.

1. The neural ODE model with 20K parameters is very small. The size is the same as a 2-layer MLP with hidden width of 200 for MNIST dataset. This MLP can be trained in a similar amount of time using **CPU** while your model is trained on **A100 GPU**. 
2. From my understanding, the neural ODE (20K) is not your proposed model. The size of your models (Lurie Net and GLN) is still very tiny 2 - 8K.
3. The largest dataset is 30-dimensional synthetic data.

**With A100 at hand, why not try some realistic high-dimensional datasets and large models.**

**The experiments are done only for the low-dimensional systems. Results for high-dimensional systems could demonstrate how much imposing the k-contraction property increases sample efficiency with limited data.**

**Experimental results for the proposed parameterization of GLN (in Thm. 7) are missing. Practical examples would help the readers understand the value of the extension to GLN.**

Before the end of the discussion period, we plan to add a larger graph coupled Hopfield Network as an example which we hope will alleviate some of the concerns regarding scalability and will also demonstrate the GLN. This example is motivated by the interaction between different brain areas as highlighted in Ref. 2.

**This is a minor error, but the notation [i, j] for integers i,j is used differently from its definition in Section 2.1 to indicate a continuous interval in the experiment section.**

Thank you for pointing this out, we have addressed this in the manuscript.

**Lack of comparisons with well-established time-series datasets and with well-established architectures. The premise of Lurie network is the generalization of other time-series architectures such as LSSM, Antisymmetric RNN, etc. However, the presented experiments did not compare the performance of Lurie network with those architectures (except Lipschitz RNN) and with the datasets where those architectures were tested on.**

The purpose of using these datasets was to highlight the different types of convergent behaviours our model can learn and to show that, unlike the other architectures, its representation robustly models the long-term behaviour even when the initial condition is subject to noise and sampled outside the training distribution. As our approach is limited to time-invariant dynamical systems, different datasets were required to the ones these architectures were tested on.

 The architectures which we compared against were chosen as they included a range of recurrent/feed-forward and stability-constrained/unconstrained models. The reason for not including S4 and the Antisymmetric RNN in the experimental results was that we expect them to perform worse than the Lipschitz RNN and SVD Combo Network on these tasks. This was explained for the Antisymmetric RNN in the first paragraph of Section 6.  As mentioned, the A-matrix of S4 takes the form of a Hippo matrix which is designed to memorise the input signal. Of course, on the tasks we are considering, this would not make much sense as they do not permit external inputs.

We thank the reviewer for their comments.

**The paper is impacted by presenting only very simple example problems. The experiments are applied to 3 degree of freedom first order ODEs that are arbitrary and not very commonly studied. The models only have 87 parameters. Trivial problems are good if the main contribution of the paper is a key insight about ML. However, the paper purports itself to demonstrate a new architecture that is proven to be superior with empirical demonstration of superior performance. For that type of claim, “serious” benchmarks for systems that are difficult to learn, due to stiffness or complexity, are required. E.g., Lipschitz RNN did sequential MNIST, audio prediction, and adversarial robustness.**

**Further, the problems are so small and simple that the proofs do not seem relevant. None of the problems demonstrate the necessity or improvement of the architecture. Would a naive model not be able to learn those systems?**

It is well-known that nonlinear dynamical systems, even those of low order, may exhibit complex stability properties, so we would argue that proofs of certain types of behaviour are still important. Furthermore, even on these low-dimensional examples, our model was the only one which consistently learnt a representation that respected the different long-term convergence property of the three systems. This is highlighted by the illustrative figures in the appendix and comparing the degradation in MSE from the best models in Table 1 to the MSE in Table 2, where the initial conditions were sampled outside the domain of the training data and were perturbed by additive noise. Under these conditions, the error between the predicted and true trajectory may increase during the initial transient, but a good model should retain an accurate prediction of the long-term behaviour. This is what the k-contraction conditions and parametrisations guarantee. We also include two naïve, unconstrained models – the unconstrained Lurie Network and the NeuralODE. Our experiments show that neither of these models were able to maintain reliable prediction.

I am not convinced by the authors' response. 

1. Let's look at the neural vector field $f:x\rightarrow \dot{x}$ which is given by $f(x)=Ax+B\Phi(Cx) $. It is clear that $f$ is a very shallow network. Therefore, its model expressivity is very limited compared with $\hat{f}(x)=\mathrm{MLP}(x):=W_K\Phi(W_{K-1}\Phi(\cdots\Phi(W_1x)))$ 

2.  In the authors' Response, the cascade structure in (A,B,C) tries to decompose the feature space $x(t)$ into many subspace $x(t)=(x_1(t), x_2(t), \ldots, x_K(t))$ and then create some layered network interaction on those subspace. It is totally different from $\hat{f}(x)$ which is a complete graph on $x(t)$. Moreover, as pointed out by Response 1, the main focus of this work is to learn a nonlinear dynamics not the mapping $x(0)\rightarrow x(T)$. Just consider a simple application, the vector field regression problem with dataset $(x^i, \dot{x}^i)$. Your model set $f$ has poor expressivity despite the learned vector fields can provide stability guarantees.

3. The model $\dot{x}=\hat{f}(x)$ can be represented by an neural ODE with implicit $\bar f$ defined as follows (see also [4]):
$$ \dot{x} =Ax+Bu, \quad y=Cx+Du, \quad u= \Phi(y)$$
where one can encode the multi-layer structure into the feed-through matrix $D$. In your model, $D$ is simple zero, and thus it not straightforward to me that how to represent $\hat{f}(x)$ using $f(x)$. 

[4] Martinelli et. al. Unconstrained parametrization of dissipative and contracting neural ordinary differential equations, IEEE/CDC 2023.

**Page 3: What is y?**

This is the input to the nonlinearity. It is an affine function of the Lurie Networks state. Please see Equation (2).

**What is \Phi? and \phi? Its definition seems to change**

\Phi is a vector function, defined by the element-wise application of the slope restricted scalar function \phi. This was introduced below Equation (2), in the first paragraph of Section 3. We have now highlighted the same scalar function is used throughout the paper and made some changes to Section 3.1, where this comment made us aware of an abuse of this notation.  

**Is Appendix A novel work? Or just a summary of well known results? A few background definitions and references are nice, but 5 pages is excessive for a conference paper with an 8 page limit.**

It is a summary of existing results (see lines 704-710); however, as these results are not well-known, we included them so that the manuscript was self-contained. 

**What does the loss trajectory show that is not reflected in the tables? There is also nothing meaningful to say about the loss trajectory.**

We disagree that it isn’t meaningful. The plots show the k-contracting Lurie Network consistently has low variance and fast convergence across the three examples, when compared to the other models.

Firstly, we would like to thank the reviewers for their comments and feedback over the course of the discussion period. We have just submitted the final draft so we thought it we would provide a summary of the main changes we have made. Most of the updates were too the empirical section of the paper, but there were also a couple of smaller theoretical extensions which we detail first:

- In response to the comments from Reviewer wY7E we have added a section called 'Relationship Between Lurie Networks and Deep Feedforward Models' where we have shown how the sparse structures of a Lurie Network can approximate these deep models as special cases. We also extended the analysis in the comments section to also account for the biases of the feedforward model. The intention here is to highlight the expressive power of the Lurie Network which appeared to be a shared concern.

- On a similar note, we added a paragraph to the related work highlighting the connection to the Implicit and Equilibrium Networks.

- Also in response to Reviewer wY7E, we have extended Theorem 7 to include graph coupling matrices which are not just boundary conditions of (7). The constraint $(G_{L2} + G_{L2}^{\top})^{[k]} \preceq 0$ in (11) is a generalised version of the negative semi definite constraint on X, as discussed in the comments. This is equivalent to the sum of the k-largest eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix within the $k$-compound operator being less than or equal to zero whereas the negative semidefinite constraint would limit all eigenvalues to being less than or equal to zero. Remark 3 was updated to account for the special case which describes all-to-all graph coupling matrices without self-loops.

- To address the concern of Reviewer zYXG, we have added the Antisymmetric RNN as another well-established model. Recall a discussion of why this performs poorly was included in the original draft and the empirical results are in line with those expectations.

- We have added two 30-dimensional graph-coupled dynamical systems to the experimental results section. These are the referred to as the Graph-coupled Hopfield Network and Graph-coupled Attractor and are motivated by interacting memory units.  For example, the Graph-coupled Hopfield dataset was generated by simulating the dynamics of 10 Hopfield Networks randomly connected through a graph-coupling matrix which preserves the multi-stability of the system. The same was done with the Graph-coupled Attractor. The state dimension of these examples is significantly larger than what is used in the LASA dataset benchmark (where the 2d trajectories are typically stacked to form 4d or 8d trajectories) and simulated datasets like the 2, 4 or 8 link pendulum (respectively 4d, 8d or 16d trajectories). The models used typically have a parameter count in the order of thousands and the Neural ODE even has 20,903 parameters.

- Other minor edits were made throughout the paper to address the more minor concerns of each reviewer and to adhere to the page limit.

Thanks for your explanation. I think your $B$ matrix would also involve $\epsilon^{-1}$ and $C$ matrix misses some identity matrices.

- Mathematically, it may be yes that $\epsilon\rightarrow 0$ is equivalent to $\epsilon=0$. I am not familiar with singular perturbation theory for differential-algebraic equations. 
- Let's assume it is yes. Then, by substituting the above $(A,B,C)$ into the current condition $\mu((A+BJ_{\Phi}C)^{[k]})\leq -\eta$, the problem of learning a deep MLP for $f$ is solved. Am I right? Can we encoding some sparse $(A,B,C)$ as above into your parameterization (9) or (10)?
- But numerically, it might be an ill-conditioned problem to learn the above $(A,B,C)$ due to $\epsilon^{-1}$.

**The Lurie network in (2) only contains a single hidden layer, which means that the model expressivity is quite limited. However, in the literature of Lurie networks [1-3], the general implicit network model contains very deep MLPs, residual networks and many other feed-forward networks as special cases.**

We strongly disagree that the model is limited. Firstly, by imposing further structure on the model parameters, in a similar manner to the Graph Lurie Network (GLN), one could construct a Lurie Network where the output of one layer influences another. Consider a cascade connection of two Lurie Networks defined by:

A = blockdiag(A1, A2), B = blockdiag(B1, B2), C = [0, C2; C1, 0]

In the above, the matrices (A1,B1,C1) represent the dynamics of the first layer and (A2,B2,C2) the dynamics of layer 2. With this structure, the output from layer 1 is influencing layer 2 as the input to the nonlinearity. The output of layer 2 is also influencing layer 1 through the same mechanism. Such a cascade connection could be leveraged to recursively assemble a model, still in the form of a Lurie Network, where different layers influence each other. 

Secondly, We would like to point the reviewer to Theorem 2 of Ref. 5, which we feel provides strong justification that a recurrent model, such as the Lurie Network, can be used to approximate any time-invariant dynamical system. Furthermore, the implicit models referenced below are alternative representations of feedforward networks, like the neural ODE we compared against, which are related to recurrent models, such as the Lurie Network, through the relationship between the implicit equation and equilibrium points of the recurrent models. As these architectures are feedforward, they are more reliant on depth for expressivity. We would also like to point the reviewer to other examples of single layer recurrent models which empirically support this claim (see Refs. 2,3,4).

Sorry for my confusing question. Let me put it in a more clear way:

- Thm.5 \& 6 show that the parameterized model $(A,B,C)\in \Omega_2(g,k)$. My question is that does your parameterization covers all models inside $\Omega_2(g,k)$? In other words, given a model $(A,B,C)\in \Omega_2(g,k)$, can it represented by (9) or (10)?

- Regarding the model parameterization, I have a new question about Thm. 7. 
$$ L=G_L-P^{-1}G_L^\top P$$
The above $L$ is an element of $\Omega_4(k, P)$. But it is a boundary point of $\Omega_4$, which can be concluded from its proof (line 1089). I guess it can be easily fixed by 
$$ L=G_L-P^{-1}G_L^\top P - P^{-1} X$$
where $X\succeq 0$ to make sure the L.H.S. of line 1089 $\preceq 0$ rather than $=0$.

**The theoretic contribution is incremental as it involves application of k-contraction theory (Wu et al. 2022) to a simple neural ODE, i.e., the SDP formulations in (4) and (7) follow directly from Theorem 1. The model parameterization method is nice, but a similar pipeline has already established in [3] for contraction analysis (k=1).**

We strongly refute this claim for the following reasons:
1. While Theorem 1 from Wu et al is the fundamental result which needs to be verified to guarantee k-contraction of the model, we have given new SDP conditions which verify k-contraction specifically for (2) in a form which can be parametrised. 
2. We would also argue that the model parametrisation of a k-contracting system is significantly more difficult than a 1-contracting system since the constraints such as (3), (4) and (7) involve the summation of the k-largest eigenvalues (in the 1-contraction case this only depends on the largest eigenvalue) or are linear matrix inequalities involving k-compound matrices (no k-compound matrices in the 1-contraction case). This makes both the k-contraction results and the parametrisations significantly more difficult to prove/design. Appendix A provides a brief and self-contained background on k-compound matrices which we also believe highlights why our results are more than incremental extensions.

summary.value: This paper studies the problem of learning dynamical systems with convergence guarantees. Specifically, it enforces the k-contraction property on Lurie Networks by finding sufficient conditions on the parameters to guarantee the property and constructing the network with parameterizations that inherently satisfy the sufficient conditions. Their parameterizations allow unconstrained optimization of the parameters to train the model. The results are extended to construct a Graph Lurie Network to find more efficient parameterization to guarantee the k-contraction property for the multiple dependent Lurie Networks rather than just treating them as a giant aggregated Lurie Network. Experimental results show that enforcing the k-contraction property improves accuracy, generalization, and robustness on various benchmarks.

strengths.value: The paper is well-written and easy to follow. The authors clearly deliver the main benefits and drawbacks of each sufficient condition they established. The experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed architectures evidently.

weaknesses.value:
The proposed parameterizations are sufficient to guarantee the sufficient conditions for the k-contraction property. However, it is unclear how restrictive the parameterizations are in expressing any Lurie Networks that satisfy the k-contraction property. Any explanation or intuition for this point would be helpful in understanding the power of the proposed architecture.

The experiments are done only for the low-dimensional systems. Results for high-dimensional systems could demonstrate how much imposing the k-contraction property increases sample efficiency with limited data.

Experimental results for the proposed parameterization of GLN (in Thm. 7) are missing. Practical examples would help the readers understand the value of the extension to GLN.

This is a minor error, but the notation [i, j] for integers i,j is used differently from its definition in Section 2.1 to indicate a continuous interval in the experiment section.

comment.value:
Thank you for your comments and feedback on our submission. We appreciate the time and effort you've taken to review our paper. We will directly respond to your individual concerns and questions, but first we would like to address some shared concerns and reiterate some important aspects of the work.

Our work has focused on providing contraction-based stability guarantees for time-invariant nonlinear dynamical systems. Previous research, for reasons of robustness and generalisation, has studied the 1-contraction property (e.g. Ref. 1 and Ref. 2 below). As 1-contraction only accounts for dynamics which globally converge to a unique trajectory, we have developed stability results and parametrisations which account for a much richer set of dynamics by generalising this beyond just 1-contraction to incorporate other forms of convergence such as those described by 2-contraction and 3-contraction: this generalisation is considerably more involved that 1-contraction, but extends notions of stability beyond fixed points to include many other forms of convergence. Throughout the paper, we have also tried to highlight why the generalisation to k-contraction is of interest in Neuroscience and ML more generally. 

A common complaint which most reviewers had was that the examples were relatively simple. While this is true, we would argue that the application of our approach to low-order examples revealed some interesting aspects of our work, principally its ability to learn accurately when other approaches failed. We will try to add a high-dimensional Graph Lurie Network example before the end of the discussion period. We hope this will alleviate some of the concerns related to scalability.

1.	https://openreview.net/pdf?id=iAYIRHOYy8
2.	https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/file/c4d5e998372e2b8742c6dc806e38bc0e-Paper-Conference.pdf
3.	https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.12070
4.	https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.09689
5.	https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/11840817_66

Sidenote: When referring to Refs. 1-5 in the individual responses, we mean the references above, not from the manuscript. We have also uploaded an edited version of the manuscript to try to better highlight these points. The edits are in red text which will be removed prior to the final upload.

1. It is quite difficult to give a quantitative answer to this. The conditions have only been proven as sufficient; however, they certainly cover a large proportion of the set. The full set of matrices B, C are modelled through the singular value decomposition. In (9), some conservatism was introduced when we placed a uniform negative upper bound on each eigenvalue of $A + A^{T}$. In (10), we let the first k-eigenvalues to be unconstrained and placed a stronger constraint on the kth eigenvalue. The main difference between the two is that (9) can model A matrices where the real component of each eigenvalue is negative and of similar value, whereas (10) can model those where some of the eigenvalues have positive real components.

2. Yes, Theorem 7 is certainly a boundary condition and we agree, adding the term $P^{-1}X$ would fix this issue (thank you for pointing this out!). Our motivation for restricting to the boundary condition was that we could remove the self-loops from the graph structure easily. When $P^{-1}X$ is included, it is difficult to ensure $X \succeq 0$ when the self-loops are no longer present. If the reviewer would prefer, we could modify Th.7 and Remark 3 to reflect this, as we agree it is a more general result.

We thank the reviewer for the informative comments and helping us to improve the quality of our work.

**The presented architecture does not take external inputs. The network that is represented as x˙=Ax+BΦ(Cx+by)+bx does not allow any external inputs (e.g., u(t) in LSSM and Neural Oscillator) from the another layer to influence the output of the presented layer.**

We agree, the Lurie Network does not allow external inputs. However, by imposing further structure on the model parameters, in a similar manner to the Graph Lurie Network, one could construct a Lurie Network where the output of one layer influences another. Consider a cascade connection of two Lurie Networks defined by:

A = blockdiag(A1, A2), B = blockdiag(B1, B2), C = [0, C2; C1, 0]

In the above, the matrices (A1,B1,C1) represent the dynamics of the first layer and (A2,B2,C2) the dynamics of layer 2. With this structure, the output from layer 1 is influencing layer 2 as the input to the nonlinearity. The output of layer 2 is also influencing layer 1 through the same mechanism. Additional layers can be cascaded in a similar fashion. 

We would also like to highlight that there are several examples from the literature of recurrent models (Refs. 2-4 to name a few) which perform well on a range of tasks but are not incorporated into deep models.

Thanks for your response. I agree with the authors that the SDP formulation for $k$-contraction is definitely something new. However, the technique contribution could be further enhanced if the authors can extend the current results from single-layer network to multi-layer network.

- Applying the fundamental result of Wu et al on your model leads to 
$$ \mu(J_f^{[k]})=\mu((A+BJ_{\Phi}C)^{[k]})\leq -\eta <0. $$
Since there exists some SDP formulations for the matrix measure bound and $J_{\Phi}$ is a semi-definite diagonal matrix, it is not that hard to obtain an SDP formulation for the above condition with a constant metric $P$. As pointed out in my previous reply, a single-layer model $f$ is not practically useful. So it will be great if you can extend your SDP formulation to the MLP case, i.e.,
$$ \mu((A+W_K J_K W_{K-1}\cdots J_1 W_1)^{[k]})\leq -\eta.$$
If so, I guess the SDP formulation can also be applied to the more general case with the implicit network $\bar{f}$.

We agree, the cascade does not help with modelling time-varying systems; that is why we have limited our application domain to time-invariant dynamical systems which we have argued is still a large class of systems of interest. For example, see other contraction related work for robotics which have also made this assumption.

[1] https://openreview.net/pdf?id=iAYIRHOYy8

[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08090

Like the examples above, our approach cannot handle systems with time-varying inputs, however we agree this would be an important extension. 

The cascade was mentioned to address the following part of your comment

**The other layers like LSSM can be a part of a bigger neural network by taking the output from other layer as the inputs (u(t)), while the presented Lurie network can't.**

The cascade shows how the output of one layer of a Lurie Network can influence another.

**I'm waiting for that :)**

Hopefully, not too much longer :)

**When we are learning unknown systems, how should we decide the value k?**

We assume no knowledge of the specific system dynamics, only some asymptotic information about its convergence. However, if the value of k is truly unknown then k would need to be treated as a hyperparameter and included in a sweep. As we are only interested in the cases k=1,2,3, we believe this is a relatively small space to perform a hyperparameter sweep over, compared to other models, and is worth the gain is robustness and generalisation.

**In the experiments, why the biases of the Lurie Networks were set to zero for some tasks?**

Thank you for pointing this out – we apologise as this should have been updated before the final submission. Prior to the final iteration of our experiments, we were testing the effect of the biases on training convergence. In these experiments we empirically found that when the biases were not needed, they significantly slowed down the training time. This was also true for the Lipschitz RNN and SVD Combo. In the final iteration of the experiments, we initialised the biases as zero for all relevant models. We have altered the manuscript to reflect this.

We thank the reviewer for the accurate comments and the appreciation of our work.

**The proposed parameterizations are sufficient to guarantee the sufficient conditions for the k-contraction property. However, it is unclear how restrictive the parameterizations are in expressing any Lurie Networks that satisfy the k-contraction property. Any explanation or intuition for this point would be helpful in understanding the power of the proposed architecture.**

The reviewer is correct, there are two sources of potential conservatism: (i) the sufficient conditions for the k-contraction property and (ii) the parametrisations themselves which are also sufficient. We provide some details on each below.

i. As highlighted in Theorem 1, P could be any symmetric, positive definite matrix, so only systems which are k-contracting in the subset P=pI can be found by our results. For k=1, it is common to find sufficient conditions in a diagonal metric. Due to the troublesome compound matrices, Theorem 3 is, as far as we are aware, the first result to prove k-contraction in a diagonal metric, albeit in an unsatisfactory manner. There is some explanation of this source of conservatism on lines 142-148 and 229-234, but we are actively working on extending this. 

ii. In Theorem 5, the only source of conservatism is introduced by placing a uniform and negative upper bound on the individual eigenvalues of the symmetric component of A. This makes the parametrisation tractable but replaces an upper bound on the sum of the k largest eigenvalues of the symmetric component of A (i.e., from alpha_k). Theorem 6 lets the largest (k-1) eigenvalues be unconstrained whilst eigenvalue k must ensure Theorem 2 is satisfied. We have added further details on the conservatism introduced through the parametrisations after Remark 2.

**The non-existence of external input (as in my previous point above) makes the claims of Lurie network being a generalized form of other architecture (e.g., LSSM, Neural Oscillator) invalid. The other layers like LSSM can be a part of a bigger neural network by taking the output from other layer as the inputs (u(t)), while the presented Lurie network can't.**

We agree with the first part of this point and would like to highlight lines 164-166 of the original draft which we believe explains our claim as intended i.e., the Lurie Network is a generalisation of these models specifically when modelling time-invariant dynamical systems (which implies the external input u(t) is replaced by a bias term). We have made changes throughout the manuscript to try and make this clearer. 

We would also like to push back a little on the last point. The Lurie Network can form larger networks by imposing further structure on the parameters which represent different ways of connecting individual Lurie Networks together to form bigger networks. For example, the graph coupling mechanism presented in the paper and the cascade connection mentioned above. As highlighted in Ref. 2, the graph coupling structure led to significant improvement in accuracy on a range of tasks, compared to a single RNN of equal size.

Dear Reviewer,
Do you mind letting the authors know if their rebuttal has helped to address any of your concerns or questions? Thank you.
-AC

summary.value: Simple neural ODE with convergence guarantees via $k$-contraction analysis

strengths.value:
1. neural ODEs with convergence guarantees
2. $k$-contraction analysis to neural ODE could be useful for control theory and computational neuroscience

weaknesses.value:
1. Most applications of neural ODE in deep learning do not care the properties of converging to a single or a few equilibrium points. Even for those stable LSSM, the Hippo matrix construction ensures that the model converges very slow in order to achieve long-range memory. From my understanding, the model in this work may have fast converging behaviors, and thus it could suffer from the vanishing gradient issue.
2. The Lurie network in (2) only contains a single hidden layer, which means that the model expressivity is quite limited. However, in the literature of Lurie networks [1-3],  the general implicit network model contains very deep MLPs, residual networks and many other feed-forward networks as special cases. 
3. The experiments in this work use very tiny networks. The largest one only has 983 parameters.
4. The theoretic contribution is incremental as it involves application of $k$-contraction theory (Wu et al. 2022) to a simple neural ODE, i.e., the SDP formulations in (4) and (7) follow directly from Theorem 1. The model parameterization method is nice, but a similar pipeline has already established in [3] for contraction analysis ($k=1$). 
5. A few important references are missing in this paper. For example, to the best knowledge of the reviewer, Ref. [1] is the first paper to form an MLP as a Lurie system and then use incremental analysis to obtain a tight Lipschitz bound. Ref. [2] further extended it to general implicit network and Ref [3] showed the connection between implicit networks and contracting neural ODEs.

[1] Fazlyab et al. Efficient and accurate estimation of Lipschitz constants for deep neural networks, NeurIPS 2019.

[2] Ghaoui et al. Implicit deep learning, SIMODS 2021. 

[3] Revay et al. Lipschitz bounded equilibrium networks, arXiv:2010.01732.

questions.value: 1. Consider the case of $k=1$, does your parameterization (9) contain all contracting models of the form (2)?

comment.value: In my original review, I put more value on the theoretical contribution of this paper, although I raised concerns about the scalability of the method and demonstration of the GLN parameterization. After seeing other reviews and responses, I agree with other reviewers' concerns and think the large-scale GLN experiment is necessary for the completeness of the paper. Thus, I changed my score to 5 for now. I will happily increase my score once I see promising results from the experiment the authors are working on.
I have read the new submission. I concur with the assessment of wY7E. The manuscript still requires major revisions and expansion that cannot be addressed by a last minute experiment.

**A few important references are missing in this paper. For example, to the best knowledge of the reviewer, Ref. [1] is the first paper to form an MLP as a Lurie system and then use incremental analysis to obtain a tight Lipschitz bound. Ref. [2] further extended it to general implicit network and Ref [3] showed the connection between implicit networks and contracting neural ODEs.**

Thank you for making us aware of this, we have included these in Section 6 to highlight the relationship between Lurie/recurrent networks and implicit networks. 

**Consider the case of k=1, does your parameterization (9) contain all contracting models of the form (2)?**

As is typical in almost all nonlinear stability results, our conditions are sufficient, so they do not include all 1-contracting models; however, nearly all 1-contracting models which satisfy Theorem 2 (for k=1) are contained in our Theorem 6 parametrisation. 

Specifically for the case k=1, it is also likely that results from Ref. 2, which apply to (2) when A = -a*I, C=I, could be extended and would be less conservative than Theorem 2. However, as far we are aware, this is the first work to parametrise a set of k-contracting models with any form, not just (2). Furthermore, we also believe this to be the first work to parametrise 2-contracting and 3-contracting systems, generally or specifically of the form (2), which is one way this work generalises similar approaches.

summary.value: The authors present a unifying architectures for time series that represent $k$-contracting dynamics (Lurie network). The $k$-contracting dynamics are usually found in many dynamical systems. For example, $k=1$ represents stable systems with only 1 stable equilibrium points in the state-space, $k=2$ represents equilibrium points (stable & unstable) that lies on a line in the state-space, and $k=3$ represents system that can oscillate indefinitely. The authors first present a general form of Lurie network and present the analysis of the constraints of its parameters to achieve the desired value of $k$. They also present a way to represent the architecture so constrained optimization can be avoided during the optimization. Experimental results comparing (constrained and unconstrained) Lurie networks with other architectures are present for some small test cases.

strengths.value:
1. The paper presents a unifying architecture (Lurie network) to represent $k$-contracting dynamics and also its parametrization to avoid constrained optimization during the training.
2. Sound theoretical justification of the architecture's capability of representing $k$-contracting dynamics.
3. The authors also present a way to incorporate Lurie network in graph case.

weaknesses.value:
I have several major concerns and some minor concerns. The following is my major concerns:
1. The presented architecture does not take external inputs. The network that is represented as $\dot{x} = Ax + B \Phi(Cx + b_y) + b_x$ does not allow any external inputs (e.g., $u(t)$ in LSSM and Neural Oscillator) from the another layer to influence the output of the presented layer.
2. The non-existence of external input (as in my previous point above) makes the claims of Lurie network being a generalized form of other architecture (e.g., LSSM, Neural Oscillator) invalid. The other layers like LSSM can be a part of a bigger neural network by taking the output from other layer as the inputs ($u(t)$), while the presented Lurie network can't.
3. It seems like prior knowledge of the dynamics of the modelled system needs to be known (i.e., whether it's $k=1$-contracting, $k=2$, or $k=3$). This makes it hardly applicable as we would not know the dynamics of most systems of interest.
4. The performed experiments seem to be very small scale (with less than 100 parameters). This raises a scalability concern whether the network can perform well with larger parameter counts. I understand that not all research group has large-scale computing capability. However, training with ~10k parameters or above should be done relatively quickly with a GPU.
5. Lack of comparisons with well-established time-series datasets and with well-established architectures. The premise of Lurie network is the generalization of other time-series architectures such as LSSM, Antisymmetric RNN, etc. However, the presented experiments did not compare the performance of Lurie network with those architectures (except Lipschitz RNN) and with the datasets where those architectures were tested on.

My minor concerns are:
1. The notation $1e-5$ is not a scientific notation (although it's used a lot in code), instead please use $1\times 10^{-5}$

I'm happy to increase my score if my major concerns are addressed.

2. The values in Table 1 is unclear. In each cell, there are 2 rows. I assume the first row represents the mean and std of the MSE loss on test set, but the values on the 2nd row of each cell has unclear meaning. What are those?

comment.value:
**Significant details on how the model is trained are missing. What are the hyperparameters of the architecture? What is the loss function? What are the labels that are used? Is the label dx/dt, or is the loss function on next timestep prediction? Which ML libraries are used? What is the HPC system that was used? CPUs/GPUs/TPUs?**

1. The only model hyperparameters are k and the state dimension, n=m, which is assumed to be known by all models, as this is the dimension of the initial condition i.e., the input to the models (Section 5, paragraph 3).

2. The loss function is the MSE – this is detailed in Table 3 (Appendix C.2) and referenced on lines 396-397. 

3. With respect to (2), the input to the model is the initial condition, x(0). The model then predicts the corresponding trajectory by integrating over the 20 second time horizon. The MSE is taken between this prediction, x(t), and the ground truth trajectory, which is the target passed into the MSE loss (Section 5, paragraph 2).

4. Since the associated code was included as supplementary material in the submission, we did not deem it essential to include details about the ML libraries in the manuscript. 

5. We have added some detail about the hardware used for training to Section C.2 and in the Table 1 caption.

**The performed experiments seem to be very small scale (with less than 100 parameters). This raises a scalability concern whether the network can perform well with larger parameter counts. I understand that not all research group has large-scale computing capability. However, training with ~10k parameters or above should be done relatively quickly with a GPU.**

We agree that the issue of scalability has not been addressed experimentally; the primary motivation was to highlight that, even for small scale experiments, many existing models struggle to learn representations which respect the convergence properties mentioned in this paper. We believe this is something which is overlooked and hence, decided to prioritise this issue for our experimentation. We hope to add a higher dimensional example of a graph-coupled Hopfield Network before the end of the discussion period, which will hopefully address some of the scalability concerns.
